messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Dat had spent thirty-two years as a public defender, accustomed to the controlled chaos of courtrooms and the quiet weight of case files. Then came the night his daughter, Linh, never returned from the downtown courthouse where they had agreed to meet. When Dat finally found her slumped against a concrete pillar, her breathing shallow after a desperate struggle, the world fractured. The memory did not arrive as a coherent story but as jagged, disconnected fragments: the scuff of boots on wet pavement, the metallic taste of fear, the distant wail of a siren that never seemed to reach them in time. Those fragments settled into his mind not as a timeline, but as scattered shards that refused to align. In the weeks that followed, those disjointed pieces began to bleed into his waking hours. Whenever he closed his eyes, the auditory echoes of that night—the heavy footsteps, the sharp intake of breath, the sickening thud of a body hitting the ground—would rise unbidden, pulling the grief of her near-loss into a crushing wave that left him gasping on the edge of his bed. Because the fragmented recall kept returning with such visceral force, it directly shaped his coping habits. Unable to bear the psychological noise, he began avoiding media entirely, turning away from news broadcasts or shelving crime novels the moment he sensed a headline might surface. Over the months, Dat’s hypervigilance toward people hardened into a constant scanning of every room. He sat with his back to the wall in his firm’s breakroom, his eyes tracking every entrance as if dangerous people were waiting to materialize. This relentless scanning was exhausting, and the fatigue naturally spilled into his daily routines. When the tension became unbearable, he would retreat to his car and consume large portions of comfort food, eating much more than usual to dull the mental noise. The negative emotions that accompanied these episodes—guilt over failing to protect Linh, shame over his own frozen response, and raw terror—flooded his system, convincing him that danger was still present. These perceived threats immediately dictated his behavior. A simple knock on his apartment door would set off a fresh wave of false alarms, his heart hammering as he was certain he was in imminent danger. In response to that spike of fear, he found himself driven to the entryway to repeatedly check that doors and windows were locked. The rigid checking provided a fleeting sense of control, but it also left a vacuum in his psychological processing. As the months turned into a year, the strategies he deployed to survive began to reshape his illness. By refusing to engage with the outside world or allow himself to rest, he starved his mind of the coherence it needed to process what had happened. Consequently, the overeating and media avoidance fractured his recall further, sending him back to the disjointed pieces of his daughter’s assault with renewed distress. The auditory recall would flare anew, the grief on recall washing over him until he had to step into the hallway, leaning against the cool plaster to steady himself. Dat’s work required sharp focus, but the false alarms that now dominated his days eroded his concentration at the firm. Colleagues noticed the distance in his eyes during strategy meetings, and the occupational consequences mounted as he stopped answering calls from former clients, convinced the world was fundamentally unsafe. He knew the danger was gone, yet the physiological alarm felt so real that it demanded immediate action. Each time he caught himself flipping to another channel, the act of avoidance temporarily quieted the threat, but it also left a hollow space that he quickly tried to fill. The overeating and hypervigilance did not heal the memory; they fed the fragmentation, which only magnified the threat responses he was desperate to escape. Now, at sixty-eight, Dat sits in the quiet of his therapist’s office, his hands clasped tightly together. He has come to the appointment because the fragmented pieces of that night no longer stay in the past, and the fear that he will fail to protect those he loves is what finally drove him through the door. What he hopes for, more than anything, is a way to quiet the false alarms and reclaim the life that has been shrinking around him.
